Past cyclesEvery term since 1943, lined up on its own election day

Both major parties’ primary votes are at record lows for this point in a term

Eighteen months after the 2025 election, Labor’s primary vote is the lowest of any government at the same point since 1943, and the Coalition’s is the lowest of any opposition. Add One Nation’s vote to the Coalition’s, though, and the total is the third highest on record at this stage. Even so, after preferences Labor’s 51.0% sits in the middle half of past governments at this point.

Note: Each term is lined up on its own election day, so month 18 is the same distance into every one of them. Past terms are averaged month by month the way this term is; where a term changed leader, its line follows whoever held the office. Comparing with governments that were re-elected or ousted adds context, not a forecast. Preferred-PM and net-approval ratings add little or no predictive value on top of voting-intention data.

Two-party preferredImplied from each poll’s primary votes, on the flows counted at the election that opened its term

After preferences, Labor is on a par with governments that went on to be re-elected

Its 51.0% is 0.5 points above the average government 18 months in. Governments later re-elected averaged 51.0% at this point; the eight ousted averaged 49.0%.

No opposition has lost as much of its vote this early as the Coalition has

The Coalition is down 9.1 points since the election, to 22.7%; by this stage the average opposition had gained 1.4. Labor is down 8.3, to 26.3%. Two governments had lost more by now.

Albanese’s net approval is below the average prime minister’s at this point

At −23.5 he is 26.0 points below the average prime minister 18 months in. He still leads as preferred PM by 0.9 points, 16.4 below the average, and Taylor, at −4.6, rates better than opposition leaders usually do.

Preferred prime minister

The prime minister’s lead over the opposition leader on the question of who would make the better PM. Asked since 1984.

Opposition leader’s net approval

How the final polls have doneEach pollster’s last two-party figure in the 14 days before polling day, against the result

Score

The final polls have missed the result by 1.4 points on average, and not always the same way

In 2025 all ten pollsters understated Labor, by 2.9 points on average; in 2019 all five overstated it. Because misses run both ways, what carries over to today’s figures is their size, not their direction.

The average miss counts each election once; a pollster’s figures count its own final polls. Lean is the average miss with its direction kept, coloured from half a point. Wrong side ahead means the two-party vote, not the seats; the six polls at exactly 50–50 count neither way. Closest and furthest rank only elections with more than one pollster. Results themselves have sat 2.2 points from 50–50 on average.

ReachTEL and Galaxy have come closest; Ipsos has missed by most

Average miss ignoring direction, closest first, for pollsters with more than one election to judge on. A pollster only counts against the elections it published a final poll for, and Roy Morgan’s 23 are the longest record by far.

ReachTEL0.6 pts2 elections
Galaxy0.9 pts5 elections

Note: Exit polls are left out, and a pollster that publishes an undecided-inclusive pair is normalised first, so its arithmetic is not scored as a miss. Before 1993 Morgan was the only pollster in the field, and its figure is read through the last election’s flows, so the miss folds in drift in the flows too. YouGov MRP’s modelled 2025 wave is left off entirely – a model is not a poll, and YouGov’s later conventional poll stands as that house’s final word. Published two-party scores each final poll against the two-party figure it printed; Primaries on last-election flows re-derives a figure from the poll’s primaries and the preference flows of the previous election instead.

About this page

The modern page in old clothes

Every finding, scorecard row and chart here is the modern Past cycles page’s own, read from it each time the site is built, at each of its Compare with and Measure settings, and drawn the way a website of about 2000 would have drawn it.

More in the modern view

The modern page draws any past term on its charts, opens each scorecard row to rank every term, and downloads the polls behind them. The front page and All polls have retro views too, and so does the Electoral map.

auspol tracker is an unofficial aggregator of published federal opinion polling.

Best efforts are made to make the aggregate figures transparent, trustworthy, statistically sound, and informative, but they are, in the end, estimates only.

How the figures are built is in Info. Spot an error, a missing poll, or have any other feedback? Please let me know.

Federal polling archives I’ve located are stored here for safekeeping and convenience.
